utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes. I apologise for the delay. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Ms. Charline Pasteur, who is a graduate law student with a masters in the law of state rebuilding and fighting impunity from the Universite Aix Marseille in France. She's been with the team since March. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We are sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. Judge Morrison is indisposed, unfortunately. Shall we continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, good morning.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I just want to ask you just two very brief general questions before we go back to Srebrenica. President Karadzic was the only person who was authorised to appoint and relieve generals in the VRS, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the decree of the president of the republic generals are appointed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And this is a discretionary right, isn't it? So it's up to President Karadzic's discretion who gets appointed and when they get appointed?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are procedures involved, you know. There are personnel commissions that make proposals, then a certain time has to be spent at a particular position in a certain rank. So it's not totally his discretion. However, since he is the one who makes the appointment, it could be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Maybe I'll just read you what you said in the Krstic case at transcript 8036 in that case. You said: "It is his right, the right of the president of the republic, to appoint generals to such high positions such as the position of corps commander. It is a discretional right of the president to do that. So it's the president's discretional right to promote someone to general and it's his discretional right to appoint someone to the position of corps commander as well." Right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not challenging that now either. I'm just saying that there are certain prerequisites that have to be met by the candidate in order to get promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yesterday we were talking about directive 7. I want to now ask you some questions about happened after directive 7, the series of events leading up to Krivaja 95. Now, at paragraph 135 of your report, if you can turn to that - it's Exhibit D3864 in the English page 53, B/C/S, page 60 - you talk about detective 7/1, and you say that the reference number of directive 7/1 clearly indicates that this document continues the realisation of directive number 7 because otherwise it would have been given the number 8 or some other number instead of directive 7/1. So we can agree there is no dispute. Directive 7/1 continues the realisation of directive 7. That's what it says in your report.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have directive 7/1 in e-court. It's Exhibit P2246. It's page 4 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And there's a particular section, General, where we can see on this page that General Mladic orders planned combat battles and operations in accordance with directive number 7 around the Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves. Can you see that bit? In the very last paragraph in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's fair to say the whole point of a phrase such as "in accordance with" means that you don't have to repeat the entirety of the previous order; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous order does not have to be repeated, and it doesn't have to be that way verbatim, because directive 7 is being provided as a general document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, General, you were aware that General Mladic issued an order on the 12th of May, 1995, to the Drina Corps to separate the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa and create conditions for their liberation. You're aware of that order, are you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said yesterday that I hadn't seen that order of the Drina Corps, and indeed that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is -- this is a different order, General. Maybe I'll bring it up for you. It's Exhibit P5216. It's the 12th of May. Have you seen this order before, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you can see in the header of the order -- we'll just wait for it to come up in English. That it's an order to stabilise defence around the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa and create conditions for their liberation. So you saw this order when you were preparing your report, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you're aware that this order couldn't be implemented at the time in May because the Drina Corps didn't have enough resources free to undertake the operation to create conditions for the liberation of the enclaves.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Drina Corps certainly did have the resources to carry out the operation that's carried out in July 1995, because they had the forces of a reinforced brigade. The forces that were there in July 1995 certainly could have been there in May 1995 as well. Whether he was handicapped for some other reasons, that's a different matter. However, as for the operation as it was carried out, he did have the resources for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. At paragraph 346 of your report, you talk about how in your view the Krivaja 95 operation wasn't planned in advance and was a reaction to a Muslim attack on the village of Visnjica which took place on the 26th of June. When you were preparing for the Krstic case you interviewed General Zivanovic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And did General Zivanovic tell you during that interview that the Drina Corps actually started their preparations for the attack on Srebrenica in early June 1995?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, let me just read you a little quote from a speech that General Zivanovic gave on the 12th of July, 1995, the day after the enclave had fallen, and this is from the Srebrenica trial video. The transcript is P4202, e-court page 256. So on this speech -- in this speech on 12th of July, General Zivanovic says: At the beginning of June or precisely at the end of May we started to carry out preparations and then took Zeleni Jadar and tested what the expulsion of UNPROFOR with weapons looked like. We did it the army way, and as it turned out that we had no casualties and no wounded and then slowly conditions ripened for what we did now. General, did the Defence give you a copy of this speech when you were preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You'd agree, wouldn't you, that the commander of the Drina Corps on the 12th of July, 1995, would have known exactly when his unit, his corps, started preparations for the attack on Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander could know, of course, but the question is whether he said that. Taking Zeleni Jadar was a precondition for using the Milici-Skelani road. It was under the control of UNPROFOR, Muslim forces and it could not be used, and therefore the manoeuvres and the supplies for the corps were seriously threatened. Zeleni Jadar had to be taken irrespective of Operation Krivaja 95. Of course, for a long time there had been the need to control the area between the enclaves, because these were two enclaves, not one, and they communicated mutually as if it were one, and that is not being contested that the corps was supposed to separate the two enclaves, Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I understand that, General, but the question was very specific. General Zivanovic said at the beginning of June or precisely at the end of May we started to carry out preparations. That's the commander of the Drina Corps saying they started to prepare for the attack on Srebrenica in late May, early June; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that is the case. In a broader operational sense, the taking of Zeleni Jadar is preparation, but that was the task irrespective of Krivaja 95.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think General Zivanovic was very clear, General, so we'll move on. Can you look at paragraph 321 of your report. It's Exhibit D3864, English page 123, 141 in the B/C/S. And you say: The mere fact that the Drina Corps commander refers in the preamble of the order for operational combat Krivaja 95 to directive 7 and directive 7/1 is not sufficiently convincing proof that the execution of the operation was ordered by the VRS Main Staff or President Karadzic. And then you go on in that paragraph and you list a number of different forms that the order could have taken, and you say you didn't have any of the above at your disposal about the order that actually trigger the operation. Now, you mention in there that an oral order from the VRS Main Staff commander could have been one of the ways that the operation was started; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Started, but then after the planning the decision was supposed to be brought to him for his approval. He could order -- I mean, he could call the commander and say prepare operation such and such and such at such and such a place with such and such an objective, but the commander was duty-bound after the preparation and planning to submit the decision for approval. I did not see any such thing, and on that basis, I came to the conclusion that that operation had been prepared in haste.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, the commander of the Main Staff wasn't the only person who could issue an oral order, was he? Supreme Commander could also issue an oral order to start the Srebrenica operation; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not to the corps commander, only to the commander of the Main Staff if we are going to respect military hierarchy. If we are going to disrupt the system, then it can be done, but in that case he'd have to inform the commander of the Main Staff that he had done that. I do not have any such information. Or -- or -- may I clarify? May I? Would you allow me to clarify a bit more? If the commander of the Drina Corps received oral orders from the Supreme Commander to carry out an operation, he himself was duty-bound to inform the commander of the Main Staff, but I assure you that the Supreme Commander has no need to issue orders orally unless these are corrective orders, that is to say if something is urgent. However, since this has to do with the implementation of a operation, that is never done orally. That is done in writing. So an order is issued in writing to prepare and carry out some operation, but let us say that he even did it orally. In that case the commander is duty-bound to inform his superior, and then the superior's also duty-bound to inform the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me remind you, General, of what you said in the Krstic case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can I intervene here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Radinovic, as long as the commander who was told to do something from the Supreme Commander informs the commander of the Main Staff and the commander of the Main Staff agrees with it, there's nothing wrong there. There's no disruption of singleness of command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, you said you didn't have any information about whether an oral order had been issued to start the attack on Srebrenica. If you did have information about who issued an oral order to start the Srebrenica operation, you'd take that into account in determining -- in determining who had ordered this operation in the first place, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you this: I know that at the time there was talk about Karadzic having said that he had ordered Krivaja 95 operation to be carried out. This looked to me as a rather PR way to settle accounts with Mladic rather than a very serious warning coming from the Supreme Command. This is not the way things are being done. Since I never found any proof of that, I simply ignored it, but I did hear these rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So let me clarify. The rumours you're talking about, this would include President Karadzic's speech to the 52nd Assembly session where he says: "I ordered in verbal and written form to attack Zepa and Srebrenica." It includes that; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw anything in writing. As for this verbal statement, I was aware of that, but as I said, it seemed to me more to be a way of settling scores rather than a serious way of communicating within the system of politics and military. I presume that had that been the case, there would have been at least some written record of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, President Karadzic made that statement to the 52nd Assembly session. In the 54th Assembly session in October 1995, he said something very similar. He said: "I personally supervised the plan without the knowledge of the Main Staff, not even hiding anything, but I happened to run into General Krstic and advised him to go straight into town and pronounce the fall of Srebrenica and later we would chase the Turks around in the woods. I approved an immediate task and a radical task, and I don't regret it." So you didn't take this into account either?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't take that into account either, because it doesn't resemble anything that Karadzic had previously done, and I understood that to be a kind of fiery speech aimed at demystifying the role of Mladic in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, you reviewed some witness statements in preparation for your report, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did say that, but if you're asking me precisely, I cannot provide you an answer. If I were to see it, perhaps I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Do you recall yesterday I asked you a question about Milenko Lazic, the Drina Corps Chief of Operations and Training, who drafted that Drina Corps order with the language from directive 7 that you hadn't seen before?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that it was Lazic who signed it -- or, rather, who prepared this order. But, look, it was impossible for Lazic to made his own plan based on directive 7. He could have done that only pursuant to an order from the Main Staff because an operation can not be planned based on directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me read you a little section of Milenko Lazic's testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you do so, let me ask you, General Radinovic. You said earlier today that you heard -- you did hear some rumours, these rumours about how the Krivaja 95 was prepared, discussed. Could you explain a little bit further about what you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard of it. I knew of it. I read about it to the effect that Karadzic had said that he didn't understand why we were turning Mladic into a legend whilst we have such a remarkable general such as General Krstic, who under my direct supervision prepared Krivaja 95 and carried it out in an excellent manner. So these are the stories that I heard. But since that was happening at the time when there was a rift which culminated between the Supreme Commander and the commander of the Main Staff, I didn't perceive that to be a normal way of communicating, and that is why I understood it in that context as I explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know Mr. Salapura testified here at the end of last month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know him personally. He knows who I am, and I know who he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He testified to the effect that at the time or before Krivaja 95 was prepared in Drina Corps, Mr. Karadzic visited directly in person the Drina Corps and gave some assignment. Did you by any chance run into any such information while preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, let me put to you part of the evidence that Milenko Lazic gave in a different case at this Tribunal. This is in the Popovic case at transcript page 21727. Milenko Lazic said: "That operation which was aimed at ending firing from those areas was initiated in late June 1995 when the president came to the corps command from somewhere. President Karadzic, accompanied by the president of the assembly, Krajisnik, and his wife, and of course the entourage that remained afterwards. I was in the operations room on duty and the person on duty at the gate informed me that President Karadzic had entered the command building. I came out. They were already in the corridor. I submitted a report and he asked that we sit down somewhere." He then says: "We sat down in the room immediately next to the operations room. We offered them if you want to drink something as hosts. He said, Yes, coffee is all right. And then he immediately asked that we summon Krstic, Colonel Krstic. He was a colonel at the time. I called Colonel Krstic and when he came they stood up, they said hello to Colonel Krstic, they kissed, and then we sat down facing one another and the talks started. President Karadzic asked, How long do you need to set off for Srebrenica, and Krstic said then, Depending on the objective preparations could take three to five days, and President Karadzic said, Well, try to make that as short as possible, which we understood to mean that as soon as the preparations were completed, that task needed to be carried out. After that we spoke informally for a little bit with the president and then I left the command building. Colonel Krstic saw the president out, and then after seeing the president out Colonel Krstic called me to his office and said that we should start planning the operation." This statement wasn't something you had when you were preparing your report, was it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's very clear, isn't it, that President Karadzic's statements about ordering the attack on Srebrenica weren't just propaganda, were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But that was not an order, not an order. An operation cannot be carried out without an authorised order. It's one thing to start planning, and it's another thing to approve the execution of an operation. Therefore, neither Lazic nor Krstic were not supposed to carry out this operation without any approval because that would cause chaos in the army had they done that. It was possible that Karadzic's assessment was that it could be done in that manner, but it's another matter whether the conditions allow that to be done in that way and whether the Main Staff agreed with that. Now, as a military expert, if I'm looking at it, I think that there must exist documents, written orders issued to subordinates that would set in motion their activities. I never come across any such documents. Therefore, it all seems to me to be just a kind of story that has no operational strength, and that's why I understood it in the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You think it's just a story with no operational strength when the president of the republic, the Supreme Commander of the army, comes to the Drina Corps and says -- tells Colonel Krstic, try and make your preparations as short as possible, which they understood to mean as soon as the preparations were completed, the task needed to be carried out. You think that has no operational strength? That's your testimony as a military expert?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying this as a military expert that a Supreme Commander does not operate in that way. He has the subordinate Main Staff, and he communicates with them. He might circumvent them, but if he does that he has to inform the Main Staff, and if the Main Staff does not agree, then the operation will not go ahead. This is my understanding as a military expert. Whether the system was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- disrupted or not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's very clear the Main Staff did agree with the attack on Srebrenica, didn't they? General Mladic even turned up and led the entry into town himself.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't have an order from the Main Staff for the operation to be carried out. Without such an order, the Drina Corps command could not have carried out this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But they did carry out the operation, didn't they, General? There's absolutely no question about that; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But not at the time when you said. The operation was carried out after the 28th and the 26th when the 28th Division incurred -- carried out incursions in Visnjica and killed everybody, burned their houses and killed their cattle. There are documents in the archives of the BH Army where they were commended for that operation. That was the reason for this operation to go ahead, not a rift between Karadzic and Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I have Exhibit P4481 in e-court, page 3 in the English, page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Probably you may have misunderstood the question. Did you mention at the end of your answer rift between Karadzic and Mladic, although it was not reflected as Krstic in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This rift existed throughout the war, because a decision to set up an army resulted in duality of powers. The commander of the Main Staff was practically promoted to the position of Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But I don't think Mr. Mitchell's question had anything to do with the alleged rift between Mr. Karadzic and General Mladic. As suggested by Mr. Mitchell, the Krivaja 95 was triggered by Mr. Karadzic's suggestion, and then Krstic or Zivanovic informed the Main Staff, and with the approval of the Main Staff, if Drina Corps prepared the Krivaja 95 and executed. There was no problem at all. Do you agree with it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that Krivaja 95 was carried out not because Karadzic came there and said this would be something good to be done. Every commander thought and believed that these enclaves should be separated because we were incurring losses. But the operation followed the slaughter in the village of Visnjica after the 28th, and I think you can find that in the document. Sabotage groups raided the lines behind Srebrenica and Zepa, notably the village of Visnjica where about 40 people were killed. The rest of them fled. The cattle was killed, and of course this operation had to be carried out, but as a rule, the army made a whole lot of plans, and some of these plans never materialised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. General, let's just be very clear. Directive 7 ordered the Drina Corps to create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further life or survival for the inhabitants of Srebrenica. That's in March. The Drina Corps, which you saw yesterday, received this order and passed on the illegal language. The Main Staff issued directive 7/1, which ordered planned combat battles and operations around the Srebrenica enclave in accordance with directive 7. Then we see on the 12th of May General Mladic issue another order --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this sentence does not exist. There is no such sentence in directive 7, the one that you are talking about. And according to the sequence of execution, directive 7/1 is a means of operationalisation of directive 7, and if an execution is to be made it's up to 7/1. One more thing --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please start and continue his answer from the last --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Radinovic, could you kindly repeat your answer from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in directive 7/1, there is not this incriminating sentence that we are discussing that would implicate and imply illegal actions. As a directive, that operationalised directive 7, it was omitted. Directive 7/1 had a higher degree of operationalisation than directive 7. Secondly, Operation Krivaja 95, as stipulated in directive 7, was envisaged not for the Drina Corps but for the Hercegovina Corps, and it relates to completely different part of the battle-field which is the Neretva valley. It has nothing to do with the Krivaja 95 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, earlier this morning I specifically asked you about directive 7/1, and I asked you and said the whole point of a phrase like "in accordance with directive 7" means you don't have to repeat the entirety of the order. And this is what you said, this is at transcript page 3: "The previous order does not have to be repeated, and it doesn't have to be that way verbatim, because general -- directive 7 is being provided as a general document." So you specifically agreed that the previous order doesn't need to be repeated.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's still in the background as a general document; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But please, directive 7/1 does not say this, and if it doesn't, then in the executive document of the Drina Corps any action in accordance with this sentence is not permissible. This is my comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So under your theory, if President Karadzic issued an order that says obey the Geneva Conventions and that doesn't get specifically taken and repeated verbatim down the chain, it's like that was never said. Is that your theory? As if President Karadzic had never said it in the first place?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are twisting the words. The point here is what is being done with the sentence that have an indication of something illegal. If there is a hint of any illegal action, those in charge must not carry them out, and in directive 7/1 this sentence does not exist. The author of 7/1 did things properly. The commander of the Drina Corps cannot invoke directive 7/1, which does not contain the sentence in question, and as a result it would be him committing an illegal act. That is my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, General, I think directive 7/1 makes it very clear. It says in accordance with directive 7, but I think we've exhausted this topic, so we can move on. Now, let's go to the 9th of July. Now, the objectives of Krivaja 95 changed on the 9th of July when President Karadzic authorised the VRS to take over the town itself; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He agreed to their proposal. It says approved by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] Exactly, he approved it --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was translated into English. Not authorised but approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And his approval's required in his capacity as Supreme Commander because there's a substantive change in the goals of the operation; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This kind of alteration has to be endorsed because otherwise it would be a deviation from what we called the strategic concept and its implementation which is going beyond his powers. If the army crosses that line, it is up to the Supreme Commander to react.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So as a general proposition, you'd agree that a substantial change in the objective of an operation required the approval of the Supreme Commander as a general rule?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only his consent is required for that to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, one of the goals of this operation was to create conditions for the liberation of the enclave; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But do you know what that means in military terms? That means to reach the features from which you can overrun the enclave should the need for that arise but still it does not mean that the overrunning would inevitably follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But you'd agree that by the 9th of July when President Karadzic approves the take-over of Srebrenica the conditions had been created. On that date, on the 9th of July, the conditions are created for the takeover, for the liberation of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on Krstic's report and the information provided by Tolimir to the forward command post of the Drina Corps at Pribicevac, one can draw such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me ask you now about paragraph 360 of your report, what you say: You can understand the wish of the local population to leave because their troops had left and because of living conditions in the town, to say nothing of the fear of revenge after the return of local Serbs who had either fled or been expelled earlier. These are the conditions that have been created on the 9th of July, aren't they? The ABiH was militarily defeated. The living conditions in the town are terrible, and the population's in fear, and by that point everybody knows that UNPROFOR is unable to defend the enclave. They're the conditions that exist on 9 July; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those were not conditions mentioned in the report as the conditions have been created for taking the enclaves. It means that conditions were created to reach certain features that would provide favourable tactical positions to continue activities towards the enclave. That is what creating of conditions means. Whatever you said might be true, but this is not part of that statement or this position that the conditions are in place for taking over the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, what I said was true, wasn't it General? You'd agree that the conditions in the enclave were terrible. You said that in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And the population is fearful about what's going to happen to them?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course they were fearful.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] And by the 9th of July, the ABiH, the 28th Division has all but been defeated.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They launched a counter-attack on the 10th but it was of low intensity, and it was obviously a swan song of that struggle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And the first UNPROFOR DutchBat troops were taken into Bosnian Serb custody, or they were guests, as they put it, of the Bosnian Serbs as of the 8th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't switch the microphone on: "It's matter for discussion whether they were taken captive or granted protection, but I'd sooner say that they were granted protection other than kept in captivity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But be that as it may, we can agree that whether they were taken captive or granted protection, that happened on the 8th that the first UNPROFOR troops were granted protection or taken captive by the Bosnian Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. General, when somebody flees their home, flees their land, leaving all of their belongings behind because of terrible living conditions out of fear, their army's been defeated, the UN can't defend them, that's not a voluntary exercise at their will, is it, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does constitute voluntary departure on the grounds that the people involved believe that there aren't any conditions for them to live there. I can't decide whether the departure was voluntary or not. This is not within my profession. However, it was their decision ultimately to leave the town and to move out to Potocari, to the UN base there. At the time it was rational. It was reasonable. There was sporadic fighting going on, and the fact that they all gathered on the 11th in Potocari was a rational thing to do. Nothing about it was irrational. Now, how did it come about that they decide to -- decided to resettle, never to come back, those of who were the local population, of course. There were quite a few refugees there who had come from elsewhere. Srebrenica was a small town, and the population that happened to be there at the time constituted mostly of refugees who had come from elsewhere. It was to be expected that these refugees would move out. However, it was not expected that the Srebrenica inhabitants would move out. Rather, conditions were to be put in place for them to return and that's what Karadzic had in mind when he issued documents to authorities and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But we can agree, just to shorten that a lot, we can agree on 11 July all the conditions were in place. It was rational. Those people had really no other option at that point in time but to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The down was not destroyed. There was very little damage, meaning that the intensity of combat in town was very low. There was little damage, and there were conditions in place for the population to return. However, measures had to be taken to this effect. The decision that the local population took was the path of least resistance, and I think that was more than clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So in your view those people could have been allowed to return home; right? The people who all went to Potocari, they could have all returned home?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All those who were Srebrenica natives could have gone back home whether on the following day or when the damage was reconstructed, when the authority was restored to town as well as the various public services. But of course there were conditions. There were instances where the population returned under circumstances that were far worse than those in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Could I have Exhibit P4254 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, this is an intercepted conversation with General Mladic as one of the interlocutors at 12.50 on the 12th of July. And you can see here General Mladic says that: "All capitulated and surrender and we'll evacuate them all, those who want to and those who don't want to." So, General, regardless of what the Muslim population wanted, even if some of them had wanted to remain, this is the commander of the VRS Main Staff saying they're all going to be moved down, even those who want to stay. Those Muslims were never going to be able to stay in Srebrenica, were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that they did have the possibility to remain there. Subsequently you have the order issued by the president of the republic to establish a civilian authority and the civilian police force and that the population should be given the choice of deciding whether to stay or leave, and the position taken was that some of the population would return. Despite Mladic's fiery speech, some of the inhabitants --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me stop you there.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- were able to return. That was the position of the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: First it's not a fiery speech. It's an intercepted conversation; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one can give a fiery speech even in an intercept, in a telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. And General -- or President Karadzic's order that you're referring to was issued on the night of the 11th, wasn't it? So this conversation is after then?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely because Karadzic's order has come before and the authorities were established, there was absolutely a possibility for the population to stay there. And this was something that was counted on regardless of what Mladic might have said. There was the wish for the population to stay there. However, it was the decision of the inhabitants themselves to leave. All those who took part in the decision-making process both in the United Nations and the civilian population, they decided to leave. Of course, there was -- this was a decision prompted by fear, uncertainty. That's all very well. But simply put, it was their decision and their wish to leave. I'm not saying that they were happy to leave, but this was simply a decision that was theirs to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. You've talked about the fear and the living conditions being part of the reason why they moved out. Let me put to you a hypothetical. Is it still legitimate to move out those people where one party has deliberately inflicted the conditions on that town, where one party has created the fear, where one party has created the conditions, is it still legitimate to then go in and offer buses to help those people move out?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will give a hypothetical answer to a hypothetical question. The unbearable conditions were not only created by the Army of Republika Srpska but also by their army which conducted themselves the way they did. They prompted the reaction on the other side. So they are both to blame. Now, as to whether the departure was legitimate, this is not within my expertise to decide on. I'm simply stating the fact as to who took the decision to leave. That was the question that I asked myself. I didn't ask myself whether it was legitimate to move people out when conditions become unfavourable. This was not at the forefront of my mind. I only came to the conclusion that they decided to leave. There were quite a few reasons, of course, to leave, but there were also reasons to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And none of them were allowed to return, were they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a matter of it not being allowed. They decided to leave, so why would one proceed to forcibly bring people back?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just one more question on this topic and we'll move on. Paragraph 130 of your report, General, you say: One almost gets an impression that all of this had been planned in advance and carried out in July 1995, and that the basic idea behind it was precisely the above-quoted incriminatory sentence from directive 7, and that's the sentence that we have seen earlier: By planned and well thought out combat operations, create an unbearable situation of total insecurity with no hope of further survival or life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica. So, General, you yourself are acknowledging that's what directive 7 says and that's what actually happened in the operation - right? - in the Krivaja 95 operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You either didn't understand what I said or you deliberately chose not to understand it. I said as if it had materialised but, in fact, I am denying it. I'm refuting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The coincidence between what directive 7 says and what the Krivaja 95 operation actually achieved. That's what you're doing there; right? You're saying this is an extra other coincidence, but there's no connection between the two. That's what you're saying; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What is being disregarded is that the departure was done as a result of the wishes of UNPROFOR and the population. That's the only thing I pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go on. Paragraph 377 of your report. I want to ask you some questions about the separation of the men in Potocari. In paragraph 377 you say that the act of separating men of military age in order to check their identity was not illegitimate in any way, nor should it raise any doubts as to its propriety. Now, if these men were separated to check their identity, it's obviously important to actually be able to identify them; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So stripping the Muslim men of their identification doesn't actually make any sense if the aim of separating them was to identify them, does it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this sort of screening documents are normally taken from individuals to prevent them from fleeing. This is a preventative measure. The point of the matter was that they had to be identified so as to establish whether they took part in combat or not and whether they were members of the 28th Division or civilians. That was the point of what I said, that the separation was legitimate so long as that screening had to be carried out. Now, as soon as there was no screening anymore, that procedure becomes illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me understand you. You're saying taking the men's identification documents was a preventative measure to prevent them from fleeing. That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you think that's legitimate to take all the identifications?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was only temporary, until such time as checks are done to see whether they are members of the army or not, at which point the documents are returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me ask again. So you're saying it's legitimate to take the men's identifications from them.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is necessary for purposes of identification to take IDs to establish whether the persons are members of the army or not. When this is established, the documents are returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, this is what you said in the Krstic case when asked whether it was legitimate to strip the men of their identifications. This is Krstic transcript T8296. And of course I do not consider it to be legitimate. I consider it to be a crime, and of course I cannot justify it. That's what you said in that case.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a matter for a later date. At the point of separation and screening, it is necessary to take the documents. It is necessary to do so. However, when the process continued and the identification documents were taken, this, of course, was illegitimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, there's no sense whatsoever to taking someone's identification documents away from them if you're trying to identify them. The only thing that makes sense why these documents were removed was so that those prisoners could be killed; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that that's a condition, that this was a necessary precondition to indicate that killings would ensue. Unfortunately, in some cases killings did ensue, but the fact that the documents were taken is not an indicator of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: In some cases, General? In all cases; right? All of those men who were separated in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. I know that they were all killed, but not all of them were killed there. Not all of them were killed in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: No. I'll ask you about that right now. At paragraph 380 of your report, you say that the summary execution of the separated men of military age could not be automatically predicted because most were killed on 16 July 1995 in Branjevo rather than in Potocari or Bratunac where the separation was made. You would be aware of the evidence in this case that at least ten men were executed in Potocari on 12 and 13 July?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You're aware that approximately 50 Muslim men were executed in and around the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac, and that started at around 10.00 p.m. on the 12th of July, right in the middle of Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that. I don't know if it's 50 or not, but I know that it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you of course know about the mass executions at Orahovac on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You'd be aware that one of the survivors of the Orahovac execution on the 14th was separated from his family in Potocari; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So your statement that most of these separated men weren't killed until the 16th at Branjevo is inaccurate, isn't it? There were quite a lot who were killed much earlier, starting as early as the night of the 12th of July; right? Before the second day of separations had even commenced.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I merely noted the fact that not -- the majority of them were not killed in Potocari but in other places, and in that context I mentioned Branjevo where there were also military men who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Military men or prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Able-bodied men too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The only people who were killed in Branjevo were prisoners, General, right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were. These were prisoners who had been taken from Bratunac. And there were most certainly able-bodied men among them. They were those who were in the school at Kula between the 14th and the 15th, and they were executed at Branjevo, and they had been taken to Kula from Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Paragraph 413 of your report. You say that it was a completely legitimate military security action to move the prisoners from Bratunac to Zvornik. Let me read to you what you said in the Krstic case on this very same issue when you were asked about the legitimacy of sending prisoners to Zvornik, and this is T8081 in the Krstic case. You said: "It is completely contrary to the military doctrine for several reasons. Prisoners of war, in accordance with the principles of the military doctrine are not held for a lengthy period of time in combat zones but are sent to collection centres that are provided for that purpose beforehand. The VRS had such a centre at the time. It was in Bijeljina at Batkovic." So that's almost the complete opposite of what is in your report, isn't it, General? In your report here you say it's a completely legitimate military security action. In Krstic you say it's completely contrary to military doctrine. They're completely different, aren't they, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only said that holding prisoners for a long time outside of a collection centre is illegitimate. However, the transfer from Bratunac to places of protection was something that was the result of the order of the Main Staff and the commander of the Drina Corps on the 13th of July, that all prisoners should be put up in venues that are suitable for guarding them. And this was the order of the Main Staff of the 14th and the order of the commander of the Drina Corps which was identical to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: All right. Well, in your report you acknowledge Batkovici is an ICRC supervised camp - right? - supervised by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, officially it was a camp of the East Bosnia Corps, and camps are organised as per the establishment of corps. So this is something that is envisaged under the organisational structure of the unit. It was under supervision. What the quality of supervision was, I don't know, but definitely there was supervision --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Supervision by the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because that was a -- no, well, it wasn't being supervised in that sense by the Red Cross. They could have visited it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Maybe you want to look at paragraph 158 of your report. My apologies, not 158, 421. You say: Batkovic, a prisoners of war camp that was under ICRC supervision. That's all I'm asking. It was under ICRC supervision; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all right. It's -- not in the sense that the Red Cross was there all the time to exercise control and supervision. Simply that it kept an eye on it. That's the gist of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. And this is an East Bosnia Corps purpose-built prisoner of war camp; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's where exchanges were conducted out of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: All right. And Bijeljina where Batkovic is approximately 60 kilometres from Zvornik; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But Batkovic is not in Bijeljina. Rather, it's in the area of responsibility of the East Bosnia Corps which was headquartered in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: All right. We can agree, General, obviously the prisoners should have gone to Batkovic; right? Yes or no, the prisoners should have gone to Batkovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And again yes or no, we can agree none of the prisoners that were held in Bratunac on the 13th and 14th of July did go to Batkovic, did they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No means you agree with Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I confirm his negation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the time. Shall we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just this terms of timing, I think I have about 40, 45 minutes left, certainly within the hour, and Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff won't have anything after I'm finished, so we should be done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Forty minutes left out of how many hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We had a total of five hours, Mr. President. I think we have about ten minutes of that. So I'd be asking to go over by, I think, 30 to 40 minutes over our estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow you additional 30 minutes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, just before the break we agreed that the prisoners in Bratunac should have gone to Batkovic, but they didn't go to Batkovic. I want to ask you some questions now about why they were taken to Zvornik instead. The Muslim column that headed -- that left Srebrenica on the 11th was heading into Zvornik territory on the 13th, 14th, 15th, and 16th of July, wasn't it? This is the military column.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And by the 15th of July, the Zvornik Brigade was so desperate for reinforcements that they had to pull Vinko Pandurevic and his units out of Zepa and send them back to the Zvornik Brigade area; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And MUP units and Bratunac Brigade units were also sent up to Zvornik to help fight the column.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the Bratunac Brigade came somewhat later, was a bit late.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So we can agree that the prisoners weren't moved to the Zvornik area because the VRS had lots of spare resources up there; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On orders from the Main Staff and the commander of the Drina Corps on the 13th of July -- actually, it was ordered that all prisoners should be transported immediately to facilities where it would be easy to guard them, and the only facilities where it would be easy to guard them until they would be taken to Batkovic were the schools in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade, that is Grbavci, Rocevici, Petkovci, Kula, the cultural centre in Pilica, et cetera. Those were the facilities where they could be guarded, but that is en route to Batkovici. That is not outside that area or direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. Well -- so you're saying it's pursuant to a Main Staff and a Drina Corps order. In the Krstic case, at transcript 8081, you said: "It cannot be conceived why the prisoners of war at the time of the most intense fighting in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade were collected, were gathered in the area of responsibility of that brigade." So in your own words it can't even be conceived why it was done at this time of intense combat of the Zvornik -- of the Zvornik Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That time could not be avoided. You see, the order is on the 13th, and they were being put up on the 14th and 15th. So no other time could be found. And that is indeed the time when fighting culminated in the area of the Zvornik Brigade. However, the fighting on the approaches to Nezuk, well, that's where the fighting took place, so that is outside the area of immediate fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, the weather in Bosnia in the middle of July is very hot, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you know the evidence that the school gyms were overcrowded with prisoners. That men were forced in sit in each other's laps.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The schools indeed had limited capacity, gyms, classrooms, so the capacity is limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. And they didn't just have limited capacity. They had no food for the prisoners, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand the witness or hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, if you could just repeat your answer. My question was the schools had no food for the prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I wasn't saying anything then. I said that the classrooms and gyms were overcrowded, and possibly they could have been put up in classrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. In addition to the overcrowding, there was no food for those prisoners, was there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, bread and water were being brought --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] That's Potocari, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether there was enough, that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's Potocari. We're talking about the schools in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in Kula it was bread that was being brought. I'm not sure, but I think so. However, that is certainly not sufficient. We can agree that there wasn't enough food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, if these prisoners were put there, as you say, pursuant to a Main Staff and a Drina Corps order wouldn't you expect to see a train of logistics documents preparing for the reception of these prisoners in these facilities in Zvornik, food, water, medical care, and notification to the ICRC that all these prisoners are being taken there? That's what you'd expect to see; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We wouldn't expect -- or rather, we would expect if this were a timely action. However, since [Realtime transcript read in error "civilian"] the massive taking of prisoners surprised everyone totally, including UNPROFOR and the Main Staff and the Drina Corps, so no one expected that. No one expected the fall of Srebrenica, the moving out of the population, the massive taking of prisoners, and that was a total surprise. Everything that was done was done on a temporary basis to put them up temporarily at facilities where they could be guarded easily so that they could be taken to Batkovic as soon as possible. That's what it looked like, but that is not what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 7, the general said since massive taking of prisoners happened suddenly, "civilians," it says. He did not mention civilians at all.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We did not say civilians.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Something seems to be wrong there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I think line 10, Mr. President. I think the word "civilian" was interpreted as "since." I think that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That seems to be correct. Shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, you're saying now this was done on a temporary basis to put them up temporarily at facilities where they could be guarded so they can be taken to Batkovic. Batkovic as we have discussed is an ICRC-supervised camp. It's about 60 kilometres more further up the road from Zvornik. It's a specialised prisoner of war camp. Those prisoners were already on buses. Why on earth when they got to Zvornik didn't they just keep going straight to the purpose-built prisoner of war camp instead of turning off into remote villages in the Zvornik area? Moving those prisoners to Zvornik was not putting them temporarily there to move them to Batkovic afterwards, was it?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, yes, I think that this is a place where they were put up temporarily and where civilians were supposed to be separated from soldiers. As we know, the column that was moving in order to break through, it was mixed. It wasn't only military men but there were also civilians who were of military age, men. So the separation had to take place. The civilians were supposed to be returned to Muslim-controlled territory and prisoners of war were supposed to be taken to Batkovic or Batkovic, or whatever. All of that was fine. However, unfortunately that was not done and from then onwards it turned into a crime and there's nothing more to be said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me ask you one other thing. You haven't seen any other documents, 13, 14, 15, 16 July from the army or the MUP making arrangements for a front line exchange of these prisoners, have you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw reports, combat reports from the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. That I did see from the 15th to the 18th, and it says there are prisoners there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But there's nothing about a front line exchange, is there? There's no preparations whatsoever being made for a front line exchange?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There locally, no, but whether that was being prepared in Batkovic, I really do not know. There's another fact there that should be taken into account. On the 16th of July, the commander of the Zvornik Brigade opened the front for the column to pass through and on the 17th it was open. That shows that the intention was not to destroy everything, because that column could have been destroyed, but no, over 2.500 people were saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. The commander of the Zvornik Brigade didn't let anyone go from the schools that were in his area of responsibility, did he? They were all killed.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Zvornik Brigade was not in charge of these facilities because this operation was conducted by the Main Staff or, rather, the security sector, and the commander of the Zvornik Brigade was not even asked about these prisoners. What was up to him, I mean he let them go. He opened the front line, and he let this column go through, the column that was moving from Potocari -- or, rather, from Susnjari and Jaglic, and in that way he saved 2.650 persons. They could have been destroyed too. Fortunately they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, General, I don't want to spend time getting on -- getting into what Vinko Pandurevic did and didn't know on the 15th and 16th of July. You're aware of the evidence in this case about the meeting in Bratunac on the evening of 13 July, are you, between Colonel Beara from the VRS, Dragomir Vasic from the MUP, and Miroslav Deronjic, who is the civilian commissioner personally appointed by President Karadzic. You know about that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: You know the evidence is that the killing of prisoners was openly discussed at that meeting, and the only disagreement between the representative of the army, the representative of the police, and President Karadzic's hand-picked civilian commissioner was not whether the prisoners should be killed but where they should be killed. And the president's hand-picked civilian commissioner, Miroslav Deronjic, insisted that the prisoners not be killed in Bratunac. And this is the evidence in this case. He said: "I have received instructions from President Karadzic according to which the prisoners in Bratunac should be transferred to Zvornik." And that's exactly what happened, isn't it? Those prisoners were transferred from Bratunac to Zvornik. They were transported by the VRS and the MUP, and they were executed, and they were buried in the Zvornik area over the next few days; right? That's why these prisoners were moved to the Zvornik area, to be killed.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, when you ask me whether I heard about meeting where this was discussed I thought that you were talking about meetings that General Mladic had with Karremans and the representatives of the Muslim civilians and where Deronjic was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do did not know --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It was very clear. My question was: Do you know about the meeting between Colonel Beara from the VRS, Dragomir Vasic, and Miroslav Deronjic, and you said yes. How did you confuse that with General Mladic's meeting with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There may be a gap in interpretation. Let him finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, as for this meeting where killing was discussed, I never knew anything about that. To this day I don't know anything about that. I only know about the meeting that was held in Bratunac at the Fontana Hotel that was held by General Mladic together with the representatives of UNPROFOR, part of his own officers, and this other meeting with the representatives of the civilians. No killing. I did not have any information about any killings. I do apologise for having made this mistake. I rushed into saying something, but I thought that you were talking about the meetings in Bratunac at the Fontana Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me put my question to you again, General. The fate of these prisoners was decided long before they ever left Bratunac. They were taken to Zvornik for one purpose and one purpose only: They were taken there to be killed, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do not agree with that. Those who took them and who took part in that did not know that they would be killed. Those who led the operation may have known. But I would like to caution about one thing. An order of General Tolimir, information, offering accommodation for 800 prisoners on the evening of the 13th of July. So on the 13th of July, the most important person in the Main Staff as far as prisoners of war are concerned does not know that they are going to be killed and is offering accommodation in Rogatica. I don't know how juniors could have known, his juniors. At that time they certainly did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Miroslav Deronjic knew, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether Miroslav Deronjic knew, but these people from the army who escorted them, these prisoners of war, they certainly did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, don't you say in your report that they're escorted by the MUP? Dragomir Vasic from the MUP knew that those people were being taken to Zvornik to be killed.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragomir Vasic was not escorting them. Policemen escorted them, not Dragomir Vasic. Why would he have to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Dragomir Vasic is the chief of the Zvornik CJB. He's the head policeman in the area. Of course he would know if his police were moving prisoners to Zvornik; right? He'd have to know.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the police who were escorting them did not know. The police who were escorting them did not know. The officers who took part in that did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But let me ask you again. Dragomir Vasic who was at the meeting in Bratunac, he knew, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How do I know whether he knew when I don't know of this meeting that you are talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Could you look at paragraph 130 of your report, General. You refer to the Srebrenica men being captured and allegedly executed. If you take a close look at footnote number 79 where you say that the execution of the prisoners was not part of Dr. Karadzic's control authority. The prisoners were dealt with by operational commands on the ground and the Main Staff of the VRS as the supreme operational command of the army, and the situation reports that Dr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: General, can you see footnote 79 there?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And you say: "The situation reports that Dr. Karadzic received from the VRS Main Staff did not contain any information about the execution of prisoners of war as a result of which this potential crime cannot be deemed part of Dr. Radovan Karadzic's control authority." Now, you're not suggesting that the VRS Main Staff daily situation report is the only source of information that the president of the republic has, are you?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that as for the line of military command and control he did not have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But you'd agree that he could receive that information from his hand-picked civilian commissioner, Miroslav Deronjic; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have, but I don't know about that. I did not receive information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you'd agree that he could receive that information from Tomo Kovac, the deputy minister of interior; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could have, could have, but I don't have that information either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that the VRS security organs are the prime unit of the army who deal with prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is their professional responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So it makes sense that if anybody is going to be reporting on the prisoners it would be them; right? It would be the security organs.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But reporting follows the chain of command. A security officer cannot report directly to the Supreme Commander. Information gathers at the Main Staff, and then it's the Main Staff that sends a single report to the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So I take it, General, you're not aware that every day during the Srebrenica operation President Karadzic received a written report directly from the VRS Main Staff security organ, that went directly to him? You're not aware of those reports?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. P2989. It's the log-book, Pale log-book that shows every day President Karadzic got a report from the Main Staff security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So I take it, General, you're not aware that when the OTP went to inspect the presidential archive these VRS security organ reports to President Karadzic were among the documents that were missing from that archive?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that I absolutely had no insight into these presidential archives because that was not submitted to me. What is contained therein I'm not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you, Mr. Karadzic's military expert, have never seen the daily security organ reports to the president during the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, General, our case is in July 1995, there's only one individual sitting at the top of the three branches of government that were carrying out the Srebrenica operation: The VRS, the MUP, and the civilian authorities. On the 13th, 14th, and 15th of July, President Karadzic was talking or meeting with a representative from each of those branches, Miroslav Deronjic, Tomo Kovac, he spoke to the phone to General Mladic on the 13th of July, and he also received a report every day from the security organs that neither you nor the Office of the Prosecutor has ever seen. So is it still your view that President Karadzic's responsibility as Supreme Commander isn't engaged with Srebrenica purely because the daily situation reports don't contain reports of the killings? That's your expert military opinion?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're simplifying the answer and reducing it. Operation Srebrenica was not an operation that had to be approved and supervised by the Supreme Commander. It is not an operation of a lower level, and it is supervised by the corps and the Main Staff. President Karadzic is the Supreme Commander. He reacts only in terms of those powers that belong to the Supreme Command. When the operational objective of Srebrenica was changed, he agreed that Srebrenica be entered. When civilian government was supposed to be established, he did that. When the police was supposed to be established, he issued an order to establish the police. And everything that pertains to a specific situation is what he receives through combat reports. Now, whether these combat reports were done up or whether they were full, I really cannot assess. And I did not have any other facts to work on when compiling this report but on the basis of the information that was provided to me. I did not have the information that you are referring to now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Yesterday, or the first day of your testimony at transcript 41435, you testified that the media mainly reported about executions of men and boys, but it was never emphasised that those were prisoners of war. Mr. Karadzic also asked you about the locations that were mentioned in media reporting, and you said that there was mention of executions in Srebrenica which was not case. I want to show you a couple of media reports, the first one from the 21st of July -- sorry, the 17th of July on P4397. This is a media report published in "The Independent" in London. You'll see 17 July. This is describing what the reporter says looked more like a place of summary execution than of combat. He had seen footage that was aired on Serb TV, and he says: "The footage of bodies appears to support the testimony of refugees from Srebrenica who claim they saw men dragged away by Serb soldiers, heard gunshots and later saw bodies against walls or in ditches along the roadside." He then goes on to say -- the author goes on to say: "The fate of the menfolk of Srebrenica has been a concern to their family and international human rights since the enclave fell last Tuesday.
