utterances.text: No, it is not. It only encompasses what is contained in a sample of documents that I reviewed. In my book I reference these documents. I think that there were 24 documents in all. This was meant as an illustration of what it would look like if all these locations and all the various units were plotted into the map.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour. It's actually the -- when we discussed this list of 222 targets, it's actually this map that follows the next page. So no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll receive --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, could you read this? Can it be enlarged, the legend, I mean, but the Defence can also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I was told this map was the last document -- last page of the document we admitted. Is it correct? Last page of the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm not hundred per cent sure. What I meant is we discussed the list, and I know that this -- this map is the next page in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think I -- I think I did, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we see the list.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could somebody help us about the number of list?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P6449, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: A bit different. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a list, but -- yeah, with other -- with the legend is in a different place. So it's slightly -- slightly different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we mark it for identification pending English translation. Probably you need the translation of the legend. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI D3885, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we going to hear Mr. Andric's evidence or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would like to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, General. I have no further questions. Thank you for your testimony and for the effort you made in order to write this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could deal very briefly with that issue. If I could have Exhibit P4975 in e-court. Further cross-examination by Mr. Mitchell:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, this was a document you were shown earlier today. It's the 12th of August, 1995. We can go to English page 2. You can see there it's to the attention of Dr. Radovan Karadzic. If I can go to the second page in English. Sorry, first page in B/C/S, second page in English. If you concentrate on the top paragraph in English. General, can you see the part in that first paragraph where it says the freeing of Serbs detained in Muslim prisons should be solved according to the principle one for one. Can you find that part? It's in inverting commas, one for one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the interpreters it's paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You found that, General?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That means one Serb prisoner for one Muslim prisoner; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, if we scroll to -- if we go over to page 2 in the B/C/S, you'll see subheading (b) at the very top. It talks about the freeing of prisoners from prisons in Sarajevo, and it talks about 150 prisoners in the silo in Tarcin, and 50 prisoners in Sarajevo prisons. So there's 200 Serb prisoners who are going to be exchanged in three phases, and then we see in the next paragraph down it says: In the mentioned phases, the bulk of Muslims who are going to be freed, so the bulk of Muslims who are going to be exchanged will consist --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You remember, General, we're dealing with a one-for-one exchange. So 200 Serb prisoners, we're dealing with 200 Muslim prisoners. The bulk of Muslims who are going to be free will consist of one-third of the Muslim soldiers who were captured in the general area of the Sarajevo front. The required number of Muslims will be completed by the remaining Muslims captured during the activities of liberation of Srebrenica and Zepa. Well, it's very obvious from this that the remaining prisoners on the 12th of August from the liberation of Srebrenica and Zepa are something less than 200; right? That's what this means.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just for this exchange. This exchange. There may be others for others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, it's very clear. It says the required number of Muslims, this is for this one-for-one exchange of 200 will be completed by the remaining Muslims captured during the activities of the liberation of Srebrenica and Zepa. That's the remaining. That's all the prisoners remaining.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it doesn't say all the remaining ones. The remaining ones from that contingent. It doesn't say that it's going to be all the remaining prisoners. Maybe you're right, but that is not what I would infer on the basis of this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I think it's very clear, General. It says completed by the remaining Muslims. Not some remaining Muslims, the remaining Muslims. It's the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I kindly ask?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's barely legible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I kindly ask that the original be read out and that the interpreters interpret this very carefully --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Oh, if the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- up to the necessary number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If the interpreters could focus on the second paragraph in the B/C/S where it says Muslimana -- it's the last two lines of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the entire paragraph be read out carefully so that it be interpreted very carefully. I can read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we ask the witness to read out?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, General, if you could read out that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Slowly to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this it? In the mentioned stages, the bulk of the Muslims that would be freed will be a third of the Muslim soldiers who were taken prisoner at the broader area of the Sarajevo theatre of war up to the required number of Muslims. It would be the remaining Muslims taken prisoner in the activities of freeing Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, the remaining prisoners?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. One more document, General. P5226. And this is a report by General Tolimir who you said earlier today was the most senior member of the Main Staff dealing with prisoners on a daily basis. So 3rd of September, 1995. And if you'd just read -- in fact, you should read this document in its entirety, General.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If we could go over to the second page in English. General, can you see in the fourth paragraph down where General Tolimir says that: The number of captured Muslims in our prisons is smaller than the number of captured VRS members in Muslim prisons? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. And the Muslim side is blocking exchanges and making it conditional that a larger number of Muslims from the area of Srebrenica and Zepa be exchanged than the number of Muslims we have in our prisons. And again if we go over to the next page in English, I think the next page in B/C/S, you'll see General Tolimir again talking about having a smaller number of prisoners. If we can go to the second last page in English. You'll see in the third last paragraph General Tolimir is talking about that the security organs and the exchange commission chairman must avoid using parents' bitterness because it's not possible to exchange prisoners who have been imprisoned for quite some time. This is the issue of VRS soldiers in Muslim custody who can't be exchanged because the VRS doesn't have enough Muslim prisoners; right? That's the issue here.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or there are too many Serb prisoners. That might be possible too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There's more Serb prisoners than Muslim prisoners at this point; right? That's what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what is written in this document, but it doesn't mean that there were few Muslim prisoners. Maybe there were too many Serb prisoners. That cannot be seen from here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, actually, General, it can. General Tolimir says it is the result of the small number of enemy soldiers captured by our unit. So General Tolimir is saying get the message out there we only captured a small number of enemy soldiers. Can you see that in the thirst last paragraph? It's the very last sentence in that third last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I want you to look at the last paragraph. Mr. Karadzic asked you a lot of questions about the commission for exchange. General Tolimir says: The commission for the exchange of prisoners of war has all the information, and they must also inform members of the prisoners' families of this, which will prevent their unnecessary visits to the Main Staff or to the office of the president of the republic in order to exact more favourable treatment and violate the principles and priorities of a comprehensive exchange throughout the front. So, General, isn't that the case? The basic point of General Tolimir's document is that the exchange commission knows exactly why there aren't enough Muslim prisoners to exchange, and Tolimir is saying you need to manage these families better so they stop coming and bothering the Main Staff and the president with this issue about why there aren't enough prisoners; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So the president -- the office of the president and the president don't want to have to keep explaining themselves to Serb families why they can't get their soldiers back.

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you remember, don't you, the conversation, the report from Miroslav Deronjic to President Karadzic, on the evening of 13 July that we have 2.000 and more come in during the night. He knew there were thousands of prisoners. Wouldn't the solution be if President Karadzic thought that these prisoners were still alive, he could solve it on the spot, couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it cannot be done on the spot because the procedure of exchanges takes time. I was the chairman of the commission and I know what a painstaking job it is. It goes on for days and days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A lot of time is required for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I understand, but he could have said to those families, rather than saying, Don't come and bother me, he could have said, We've got thousands of prisoners from Srebrenica. Why don't we exchange them for your family members. That's what he would have said if he knew that those -- or if he thought those prisoners were still alive; right?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that he didn't tell them. He asked for the commission in charge to resolve the matter, not he.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Nothing further, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, may I just briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Further re-examination by Mr. Karadzic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, sir, could you please look at the last sentence in the penultimate paragraph where it says disregarding the impossibility of exchanging captured members of the VRS since the beginning of the war in Croatia and the former BiH. How come -- how come did that happen that there were more Serbs than Muslims? How many did I release without reciprocity from other side?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know about that. I know that our army and I was president of that commission exchanged on the basis of principle all for all, so not one for one. Not bearing in mind -- not taking into account how many were on either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Doesn't this sentence indicate that from the very beginning of the war there were captured members of the VRS in Croatia and Bosnia who hadn't been exchanged yet?

utterances.speaker: RADOVAN RADINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That was leading, Mr. President, but it's over.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, had the General just read that, that is literally what that sentence says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Once again, General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He said he didn't know that. Shall we -- shall we conclude?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence, General Radinovic. Thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, may I just -- page 95, line 17. It was not recorded that it is the commission that is in charge of exchanges, not I.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, it can be listened to and then ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That may be correct. While we are waiting for the next witness, Mr. Robinson, this is a matter we find out while checking all the pending motions. On the 14th of March this year, the Prosecution filed a motion to exclude in part the evidence of Witness Nedjo Vlaski. On the same day you informed the Chamber that this witness would be postponed. Theoretically or technically this is still pending. So I wanted to check whether the Defence is minded to call this witness, whether this witness is coming to testify, and whether the Prosecution is minded to withdraw the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That issue is still under review, so we couldn't say for sure that he's not going to be called at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could let us know as soon as that has been resolved or decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be connected to the broader issue of how many witnesses we're allowed to call before the end of our case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General Andric.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes. Before you commence your evidence, General Andric, I must let you know that a certain Rule of evidence that we have here at the Tribunal that is Rule 90(E). Under this Rule you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecution, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of guilt for a criminal offence or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question, but in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled in such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I also apologise to you for the delay due to the prolonged examination of previous witness having subpoenaed you to appear today, and it's evident we cannot conclude your evidence today, and we'll continue on Monday next week. That said, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General.

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us please pause between questions and answers, and let us speak slowly. Did you give a statement to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have 1D9091 in e-court. Please take a look, left-hand side of the screen. Do you see that statement before you?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's very small, though, but I have a copy in front of me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read and signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness please be shown the last page in order to identify his signature. General, sir, did this statement faithfully reflect what you said, or do you need to correct something?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes. Something is omitted though, my attendance at the funeral in Vlasenica on the 30th for a few hours. I went there, from the area of Milici where there was combat activity, and then I returned again to the zone of combat action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the 30th of September of which year and which paragraph does this apply to?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: The 30th of September, 1992. I apologise. I will have to take out a different -- or, rather, I'll have to take out my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it paragraph 7?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Paragraph 7, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where were you in combat at the time?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: I was in the municipality of Milici, because the Muslim forces led by Naser Oric attacked the village of Podrinje out of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The funeral of those who were killed taking place on the 30th, was it in the area where you were deployed?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: You mean the Serbs that were killed? Well, it was not in the area of my immediate deployment, but it was in the area of responsibility of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You came for the funeral. How long did you stay for?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: A very short time. After the funeral mass I went to the territory of the Milici municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Taking this into consideration, does the rest of the statement faithfully reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I tender this statement into evidence pursuant to Rule 92 ter. And Mr. Robinson will present the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We're offering four associated exhibits and none of them are on our Rule 65 ter list as we hadn't interviewed General Andric at the time that list was filed, so we ask that they be added.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Four documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. If you're looking at our revised filing for this Rule 92 ter, it's the first four documents listed in the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you name them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The first one is 1D10110.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The second is 1D09090.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The third is 02604. And the final one is 21902.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Ms. Pack?

utterances.speaker: MS. PACK
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will admit the statement as well as the four associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: So 92 ter statement 1D9091 will be Exhibit D3886, and the four associated exhibits will be Exhibits D3887 through to D3890 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue, Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will now read a short summary of the statement of General Svetozar Andric in English. [In English] On May the 19th 1992, Svetozar Andric joined the VRS and he was appointed commander of the Birac Brigade in Sekovici. He remained in this position till 6th of August, 1995, when he took over the post of the Chief of Staff of the Drina Corps. From March 1996 to July 1997, Mr. Andric was the Chief of Staff of the 3rd Corps and from July 1997 on, he was the Chief of Staff of the 5th Corps. In 1999, he was appointed commander of the 5th Corps, and he held this position until his retirement in 2002. The Birac brigade was formed on 19th of May, 1992, from parts of the units of the Territorial Defence Municipal Staff from the area of Birac. The brigade was organised exclusively on a territorial principle, since platoons, companies, and battalions were formed primarily from the local able-bodied men. The Birac Brigade had the zone of responsibility of a corps and it was therefore impossible to control such territory effectively. On 28th of May, 1992, Svetozar Andric ordered to move out the local population of Muslim ethnicity which was to be done in an organised way and in co-operation with the municipalities. This order was prompted by the fact that the brigade zone of responsibility was full of numerous armed individuals and local units under the command of the Muslim Territorial Defence Staff and local Crisis Staffs. There were also several Serbian paramilitary units that were not under the brigade's control which consequently presented a threat for both the Serbian and Muslim residents. The order to move out residents referred only to those Muslims who expressed their wish to move out. The request to move out was often motivated by fear of retaliation on the part of the Serbs evicted from the Tuzla basins after 15th of May, 1992. The security issue was impossible to control due to the large size of the brigade's zone of responsibility and to the fact that all military units were engaged on the first line. It is for these very reasons that local civilian authorities also adopted the decision to organise the transfer of the Muslim civilians. On 31st of May, 1992, Svetozar Andric ordered that a camp be established in Vlasenica stressing that international rules must be applied and forbidding any ill-treatment or liquidation of the prisoners. On 7th of June, 1992, the commander of the Eastern Bosnian Corps, of which Birac Brigade was part, ordered the respect of the Geneva Conventions with regard to the prisoners of war and strictly forbade any kind of ill-treatment of the civilians. Mr. Andric did not know that on 30th of September, 1992, prisoners of war were allegedly liquidated in Susica camp. The Birac Brigade had neither the responsibility nor the strength to protect the prisoners of war over a prolonged period of time. In December 1994, four-month truce was signed and until April 1995. The Muslims took advantage of this period of truce to additionally arm themselves with the help of the Islamic countries and to plan large-scale offensives which they publicly announced in spring 1995. Not waiting for the agreed and signed truce period to expire, the Muslim commands issued an order to the forces of the BH Army to launch an offensive on Majevica, Ozren and Vlasic. The VRS respected the truce and was in the state of strategic defensive thus managing to crush the attack. In early June 1995, the Muslims launched an offensive from the direction of Tuzla and Kladanj towards Srebrenica and Zepa. During the attack on the village of Zelina, Mr. Andric's house was burned together with the whole Serbian village of 150 houses. After the horrific crimes committed again the Serbian people in 1992 and early 1993 in the eastern part of Birac and central Podrinje, the Muslims withdrew in the general area of Srebrenica municipality. The international community proclaimed Srebrenica and subsequently also Zepa a protected zone, but UNPROFOR did nothing to carry out the demilitarisation of the area. The accord on demilitarisation and the agreement reached by General Mladic and General Halilovic on 8th of May, 1993, strictly forbade any kind of military operation. Nevertheless, in full sight of the UNPROFOR forces Muslims planned their combat activities within the enclave and carried them outside of the protected zone. During the combat actions, they disarmed by the force a part of UNPROFOR forces and used the stolen equipment against Serbs -- Serbian soldiers. Srebrenica and Zepa were supposed to be demilitarised zones and they were only formally and the VRS simply had to take some measures. The operation against Srebrenica and Zepa was launched on 5th of July, 1995. On 11th of July, Mladic, Pandurevic, Krstic, and Blagojevic held a meeting at the Bratunac Brigade command. The only decision made at this meeting was to continue operations towards Zepa and there was no mention of any liquidation or relocation of local population. Svetozar Andric did not have the impression that those present at the meeting had informed President Karadzic about the events in Srebrenica. Mr. Andric never heard General Krstic speak to anyone about the unlawful killing of the prisoners of war in Srebrenica. And that is a short summary. [Interpretation] I have only one question which will perhaps make it easier for us to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: General, in relation to Vlasenica, where is Milici located and where is Susica? Is that in the same direction or --

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Susica or, rather, the collection centre of Susica lies between Sekovici and Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And Milici where you were deployed?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: Milici is situated in the direction of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that on the same side or on the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: SVETOZAR ANDRIC
utterances.text: On the opposite side.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions for the General at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: General Andric, as you have noted, your evidence in chef in this case has been admitted in writing, that is, through your written statement in lieu of your oral testimony, and you will now be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. However, given the timing, we will adjourn for today and continue on Monday at 9.00. I'd like to advise you in the meantime you're not supposed to discuss with anybody else about your testimony. Do you understand that, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. One quick housekeeping matter. I think in his haste to complete the process Mr. Mitchell did not tender 65 ter 25423, which was the questions about which were commenced on page 49 and continued on to page 50 of the transcript. It was an article published in "Slobodna Bosna" on March 1996 that the witness confirmed the information in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have no objection to the admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Interview with Erdemovic. No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. In light of the response, we'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6451, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't hear you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that it would be helpful if the Chamber was aware of the fact that this was not a Serb magazine as Mr. Mitchell suggested. Rather, it is of an ultra anti-Serb position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. The hearing is adjourned.
